title: Shapoor Mistry Backs Tata Sons Listing as RBI Directive Clears Path
excerpt: The Shapoorji Pallonji Group chairman welcomed the Reserve Bank's refusal to let Tata Sons deregister as an NBFC, calling a public listing a bridge between private ownership and public accountability amid a deepening boardroom rift.
body:
• Shapoor Mistry, whose family owns about 18.4% of Tata Sons, welcomed the RBI's September 11 decision forcing the holding company to comply with upper-layer NBFC rules — a path toward a long-resisted public listing.
  • He said the listing could become "a bridge" between shareholders and the Tata Trusts and between private ownership and public accountability, insisting it should not be seen as one stakeholder's victory over another.
  • The SP Group argues a listing would unlock value for more than 1.2 crore indirect shareholders and secure a transparent dividend stream for the Tata Trusts' philanthropic work.
  • The comments land amid a full-blown governance crisis: the Tata Sons board reappointed N. Chandrasekaran as chairman on September 17, a move the Tata Trusts dismissed as "illegal."

The chairman of the Shapoorji Pallonji Group has thrown his weight behind a public listing of Tata Sons, describing it as a social and moral imperative after the Reserve Bank of India rejected the holding company's attempt to escape its regulatory obligations. In a statement on Thursday, Shapoor Mistry welcomed the central bank's September 11 decision to refuse Tata Sons' application to surrender its registration as a core investment company,.

Mistry, whose family is the single largest minority shareholder in Tata Sons with about 18.4% of the company, said he looked forward to working constructively with Tata Sons and the Tata Trusts on the company's future. "This landmark decision should not be viewed as a victory of one stakeholder over another," he said. "The listing of Tata Sons can become a bridge" between shareholders and the Tata Trusts, and between private ownership and public accountability.

Context & Background

The dispute traces back to the RBI's scale-based regulatory framework, introduced in October 2021, which placed Tata Sons in the "upper layer" of non-bank financial companies in September 2022 because of its borrowings and investments in group companies. Upper-layer NBFCs must list publicly — Tata Sons missed the September 30, 2025 deadline, and its 2024 attempt to voluntarily surrender its registration was never accepted by the central bank. The September 11 rejection formally closed that escape route.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=NH4Gg7R00GQ

Mistry has been the listing's most persistent advocate, calling transparency "the truest form of respect for both legacy and the future" and framing a Tata Sons IPO as "not merely a financial step, but a moral and social imperative." The SP Group argues a listing would unlock "immense" value for more than 1.2 crore shareholders of listed Tata companies, who are indirect shareholders of Tata Sons, and a defined, robust dividend stream for the Tata Trusts.

"The listing of Tata Sons can become a bridge between shareholders and the Tata Trusts and between private ownership and public accountability."

— Shapoor Mistry, Chairman, Shapoorji Pallonji Group

Impact & Analysis

The RBI's stance removes a long-standing overhang on widely held Tata equities. Reuters reported group stocks rose between 0.15% and 5% on Thursday on reports of leadership continuity, led by Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles, up 5%.

The SP Group's advocacy also serves its own balance sheet. The group has pledged its Tata Sons stake to raise debt, and the Hindu BusinessLine has reported its total debt at close to ₹60,000 crore, roughly half of it promoter-level, with about $1.2 billion due for repayment in December. A public listing would give the Mistry family a market-priced route to monetize its 18.37% holding — a powerful financial motive alongside the governance argument.

The Tata Trusts, which control 66% of Tata Sons, remain opposed. Reuters reported the Trusts have warned a listing would "destroy" the character of a group majority-owned by charities.

The Chandrasekaran Flashpoint

Mistry's statement arrived a day after the Tata Sons board approved a third five-year term for N. Chandrasekaran as executive chairman by majority vote on September 17 — reversing his own August 12 decision not to seek reappointment when his term ends on February 20, 2027. The Trusts immediately called the resolution "illegal," arguing the articles of association require both Trust-nominated directors to vote in favour, and Noel Tata, the Trusts' chairman, voted against.

Diaspora Angle

Tata group equities and ADRs sit in countless Indian-diaspora portfolios, and TCS alone is a top global holding among NRI investors. A clearer regulatory path and stronger board accountability at the holding company directly affect the value of those investments.

What's Next

All eyes are now on how Tata Sons responds to the RBI directive — listing preparations or a challenge to the regulator — and whether the Chandrasekaran standoff moves from public statements to legal proceedings. With the SP Group's December debt repayments approaching, the pressure for a negotiated exit is only building.
